newsitem.title: TURKMENISTAN: Turkmen leader pledges private land ownership.
newsitem.headline: Turkmen leader pledges private land ownership.

text.p: Turkmen leader Saparmurat Niyazov, known for his cautious approach to economic change, has handed over some state lands for private use and promised to speed the pace of land reform.

The official Neitralny Turkmenistan paper said on Monday Niyazov had handed land certificates to around 80 people at the weekend. The certificates give them eternal use of the irrigated state land but without the right to sell it.
The paper said Niyasov, who distributed a total of 730 hectares to his country's first group of owners, had promised to follow it with similar handovers nationwide.
Until now, Niyazov's nation of 4.5 million was more accustomed to his words that 'there must be no rush, and reforms must be well-thought'.
But Niyazov, the desert nation's former top communist party boss, appears seriously worried by a severe crisis hitting agriculture.
His programme to achieve self-sufficient production of food chiefly by orders hit serious problems last year, when Turkmenistan had a disastrous grains harvest.

The country, where 55 percent of the population live in the countryside, harvested a mere 400,000 tonnes of grain in 1996, way below official forecasts of 1.2 million tonnes and the previous year's harvest of 1.0 million tonnes.

Bread shortages and growing social tension forced Niyazov to raise the state purchase price of the future grain harvest three-fold, to 400,000 manats per ton, and subsidise flour supplies for the most needy.
Last week Niyazov issued a decree freeing all agricultural producers from profit tax, which averages 25 to 30 percent, from February 1.
The same decree said products made by all local agricultural producers would be exempt from value-added tax.
